title: Getting Around Town
pronunciation_focus_summary: U vs OU -- two sounds that English speakers constantly confuse. 'Rue' (street) has the French U (lips pursed forward, tongue at front). 'Route' (road) has OU (lips rounded back). Mixing them up changes meaning entirely.

phrases.text: Ou est la station de metro ?
phrases.phonetic_ipa: u ɛ la stasjɔ̃ də metʁo
phrases.phonetic_approx: oo EH lah stah-SYOHN duh may-TROH
phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Ou' uses the OU sound -- lips rounded, tongue at back (like English 'oo'). 'Station' ends with the nasal '-tion' (syohn). 'Metro' has the uvular R and a closed 'e' accent.
phrases.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, ou est la station de metro la plus proche ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'ou' in 'tournez' is the back OU vowel -- tongue at the back. 'Gauche' has the 'au' sound which is like 'oh'. The '-ez' ending is 'ay'. The 'ch' is 'sh' in French.
phrases.example_sentence: Tournez a gauche au prochain feu.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'oi' in 'droite' makes the 'wah' sound. Two French R sounds close together: one in 'tournez' and the 'dr' cluster in 'droite'. The final 'e' is silent.
phrases.example_sentence: Tournez a droite apres la boulangerie.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Tout' has the OU sound -- the final 't' is silent. 'Droit' also has a silent final 't'. The 'oi' combination always makes 'wah'. Notice 'tout' uses OU (back) -- compare with 'tu' which uses U (front).
phrases.example_sentence: Continuez tout droit pendant cinq minutes.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Loin' combines the 'oi' (wah) with a nasal vowel -- it becomes a nasalized 'wehn'. The 'n' is not pronounced separately; it nasalizes the preceding vowel. Short and very useful question.
phrases.example_sentence: Le musee, c'est loin d'ici ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'e' in 'pres' is the open E (like 'eh'). The French R in 'pres' comes right after the 'p'. 'Ici' is straightforward: ee-SEE. The 's' in 'pres' is silent.
phrases.example_sentence: Ne vous inquietez pas, c'est pres d'ici.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: THE key word for mastering the French U. 'Rue' has the French U -- lips pursed tightly forward (like whistling), tongue pushed to the front of your mouth. It is NOT the same as English 'roo'. Compare with 'roue' (wheel) which has OU.
phrases.example_sentence: La rue de Rivoli est tres connue a Paris.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Route' has OU -- lips rounded but tongue stays at the BACK of your mouth. Compare carefully: 'rue' (y -- front) vs 'route' (u -- back). The final 'e' is silent. This distinction is crucial for being understood.
phrases.example_sentence: Quelle route faut-il prendre pour aller a Lyon ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'u' in 'perdu' is the French U -- lips forward, tongue front. The 'ui' in 'suis' has the special French semi-vowel 'ew-ee' glide. The French R sits between 'pe' and 'du'. For feminine: 'perdue' (same pronunciation).
phrases.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, je suis perdu. Ou est la gare ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'e' in 'arret' is the open E ('eh'). The French R is prominent. The word 'bus' in French uses the French U, not the English 'uh' -- so it sounds more like 'boos' with pursed lips.
phrases.example_sentence: L'arret de bus est au coin de la rue.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'ill' in 'billet' makes a 'y' sound (like English 'yes'), not a 'l' sound. So it is 'bee-yeh', not 'bill-eh'. The '-et' ending is an open 'eh'. This is a common pattern: fille, famille, billet all have this 'y' sound.
phrases.example_sentence: Un billet aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plait.

phrases.text: A quelle heure part le train ?
phrases.translation: What time does the train leave?
phrases.phonetic_ipa: a kɛl œʁ paʁ lə tʁɛ̃
phrases.phonetic_approx: ah kel UHR PAHR luh TREHN
phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Heure' has the open 'eu' vowel -- like 'uh' but with rounded lips. 'Train' ends with a nasal vowel 'ehn'. Multiple R sounds: in 'heure', 'part', and 'train'. The 't' in 'part' is silent.
phrases.example_sentence: A quelle heure part le prochain train pour Paris ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Two 'ch' sounds (pronounced 'sh' in French) surrounding a French R. Practice: sh-R-sh. The 'e' is an open E. Very useful starter phrase for asking directions -- just add the place name after it.
phrases.example_sentence: Je cherche la gare Saint-Lazare. C'est par ou ?

phrases.translation: Can you show me the way?
phrases.pronunciation_notes: Two nasal vowels: the 'in' in 'm'indiquer' and the 'in' in 'chemin' -- both are the same nasal sound 'ehn'. 'Chemin' starts with 'sh' (French 'ch'). The 'ou' in 'pouvez' is the back OU vowel.
phrases.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, pouvez-vous m'indiquer le chemin pour aller au Louvre ?

phrases.text: C'est a cinq minutes a pied
phrases.phonetic_ipa: sɛt a sɛ̃k minyt a pje
phrases.phonetic_approx: set ah SAHNK mee-NOOT ah PYAY
phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'inq' in 'cinq' combines a nasal vowel with a 'k' sound. 'Minutes' has the French U. 'Pied' has a silent 'd' and the 'ied' sounds like 'yay'. Useful for understanding distance estimates.
phrases.example_sentence: Le restaurant, c'est a cinq minutes a pied.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Plan' has the nasal 'an' vowel -- 'ahn' with air through the nose, not pronouncing the 'n' separately. 'Ville' has the French 'ill' which here is pronounced as a regular 'l' (exception to the usual 'y' sound). The final 'e' is silent.
phrases.example_sentence: Est-ce que vous avez un plan de la ville ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Trouve' has the OU vowel -- back of the mouth. The French R appears in both 'trouve' and 'gare'. This is a slightly more formal way to ask 'where is' compared to 'ou est'. 'Gare' ends with the uvular R.
phrases.example_sentence: Pardon, ou se trouve la gare du Nord ?

phrases.text: Prenez la premiere rue a droite
phrases.translation: Take the first street on the right
phrases.phonetic_ipa: pʁəne la pʁəmjɛʁ ʁy a dʁwat
phrases.phonetic_approx: pruh-NAY lah pruh-MYEHR ROO ah DRWAHT
phrases.pronunciation_notes: Four French R sounds in one phrase! 'Premiere' has two R's. 'Rue' has the French U (front). 'Droite' has the R plus the 'oi' (wah) sound. This is excellent R practice in context.
phrases.example_sentence: Prenez la premiere rue a droite, puis continuez tout droit.

phrases.translation: I would like to go to...
phrases.pronunciation_notes: Liaison: the 's' in 'voudrais' links to 'aller' as a 'z' sound. 'Aller' is simple: ah-LAY. The R in 'voudrais' is uvular. Very versatile phrase -- add any destination at the end.
phrases.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, je voudrais aller a la Tour Eiffel.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'En' is the nasal 'an' vowel. 'Face' keeps the 's' sound for the 'c' (before 'e'). The final 'e' in 'face' is barely pronounced. Very useful for giving and understanding location descriptions.
phrases.example_sentence: La pharmacie est en face de la boulangerie.

dialogues.context: Asking a stranger for directions on the street

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Excusez-moi, je cherche la station de metro Chatelet. C'est par ou ?
exchanges.translation: Excuse me, I'm looking for the Chatelet metro station. Which way is it?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: ex-koo-ZAY mwah zhuh SHEHRSH lah stah-SYOHN duh may-TROH shah-TLEH. seh pahr OO

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.text: Bien sur ! Continuez tout droit sur cette rue, puis tournez a gauche a la deuxieme rue.
exchanges.translation: Of course! Continue straight on this street, then turn left at the second street.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: byehn SOOR! kohn-tee-NWAY too DRWAH soor SET ROO pwee toor-NAY ah GOHSH ah lah duh-ZYEM ROO

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.text: Non, c'est a cinq minutes a pied. Vous verrez le panneau du metro.
exchanges.translation: No, it's five minutes on foot. You'll see the metro sign.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: nohn set ah SAHNK mee-NOOT ah PYAY. voo veh-RAY luh pah-NOH doo may-TROH

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.translation: Thank you very much, that's very kind.

dialogues.notes: Always start with 'Excusez-moi' when approaching a stranger for directions. Parisians are generally willing to help if approached politely. 'C'est par ou ?' is a casual way to ask 'which way?'

dialogues.context: Buying a metro ticket at the station

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Bonjour, je voudrais un billet pour la ligne 4, s'il vous plait.
exchanges.translation: Hello, I would like a ticket for line 4, please.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: bohn-ZHOOR zhuh voo-DREH uhn bee-YEH poor lah LEE-nyuh KATR seel voo PLEH

exchanges.speaker: agent
exchanges.text: Un aller simple ou un aller-retour ?
exchanges.translation: A one-way or a round trip?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: uhn ah-LAY SEHN-pluh oo uhn ah-LAY ruh-TOOR

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.translation: A one-way. How much is it?

exchanges.speaker: agent
exchanges.text: Deux euros dix. Vous payez par carte ou en especes ?
exchanges.translation: Two euros ten. Are you paying by card or cash?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: duh uh-ROH DEESS. voo pay-YAY pahr KAHRT oo ahn ess-PESS

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Par carte, s'il vous plait. Merci.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: pahr KAHRT seel voo PLEH. mehr-SEE

dialogues.notes: In Paris, a single metro ticket (t+) works for the entire metro network regardless of distance. Consider buying a carnet (book of 10 tickets) or the Navigo Easy card for multiple trips. Most stations now have ticket machines with English language options.

dialogues.context: Lost in the city, asking for help finding your hotel

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Excusez-moi, je suis perdu. Je cherche la rue de Rivoli.
exchanges.translation: Excuse me, I'm lost. I'm looking for Rue de Rivoli.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: ex-koo-ZAY mwah zhuh SWEE pehr-DOO. zhuh SHEHRSH lah ROO duh ree-voh-LEE

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.text: La rue de Rivoli ? Ce n'est pas loin. Vous voyez le grand batiment la-bas ?
exchanges.translation: Rue de Rivoli? It's not far. Do you see the big building over there?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: lah ROO duh ree-voh-LEE? suh NEH pah LWEHN. voo vwah-YAY luh GRAHN bah-tee-MAHN lah-BAH

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.text: Alors, prenez cette rue a droite, puis la premiere a gauche. La rue de Rivoli est juste en face.
exchanges.translation: Well, take this street to the right, then the first left. Rue de Rivoli is right across.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: ah-LOHR pruh-NAY SET ROO ah DRWAHT pwee lah pruh-MYEHR ah GOHSH. lah ROO duh ree-voh-LEE eh JOOST ahn FAHSS

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.translation: Thank you so much! Have a good evening.

dialogues.notes: If you are truly lost, look for a pharmacie (pharmacy, marked with a green cross) -- pharmacists are required to help with directions. You can also enter any shop and ask politely. Downloading an offline map before your trip is highly recommended.

cultural_notes.title: Getting around in French cities
cultural_notes.content: Paris has one of the world's densest metro networks with 16 lines covering the city. Buy tickets at machines in stations -- most have English language options. The Navigo Easy card is a reloadable contactless card that simplifies travel. In smaller French cities, buses and trams are the main public transport. Taxis can be hailed at designated stands (not waved down on the street like in New York). Ride-sharing apps also work throughout France. When asking for directions, always start with 'Excusez-moi' and use 'vous' -- the French value politeness, and people are much more willing to help if approached respectfully.

cultural_notes.title: The French U sound -- why it matters
cultural_notes.content: The French U (written 'u') and OU ('ou') are entirely different sounds that can change meaning. 'Rue' (street) vs 'roue' (wheel), 'tu' (you) vs 'tout' (all/everything), 'dessus' (on top) vs 'dessous' (underneath). English has no equivalent of the French U. To produce it: say 'ee' as in 'see', then WITHOUT moving your tongue, round your lips tightly as if whistling. The tongue stays forward while the lips go round. Practice with a mirror -- if your tongue pulls back, you are making OU instead. This is one of the most important pronunciation distinctions in French.
